t: Set Intersection Size At Least Two — Greedy with Sorting
o:
We must pick the smallest set of integers so that every interval [start, end] contains at least two chosen integers. This is a classic interval-covering greedy: process intervals in a smart order and maintain the two largest chosen integers seen so far, since only those can possibly lie inside future intervals.

**Example 1** [[1,3],[3,7],[8,9]]: sort by end (ties by start descending) → [[1,3],[3,7],[8,9]]. For [1,3] we pick 2 and 3. For [3,7], both 2 and 3 are ≤ 7 but only 3 is ≥ 3, so we need one more; pick 7 (largest possible). For [8,9] nothing qualifies; pick 8 and 9. Total = 5.

**Example 2** [[1,3],[1,4],[2,5],[3,5]]: sorted → [[1,3],[1,4],[3,5],[2,5]]. Pick {2,3} for [1,3]. [1,4] already has two. [3,5] has one (3), add 5. [2,5] now has 3 and 5. Total = 3.

**Example 3** [[1,2],[2,3],[2,4],[4,5]]: sorted → [[1,2],[2,3],[2,4],[4,5]]. Pick {1,2}; [2,3] needs one more, pick 3; [2,4] has 2,3; [4,5] needs two, pick 4,5. Total = 5.

With n up to 3000, an O(n log n) sorting-based greedy is easily fast enough.
k: Sort intervals by end ascending, breaking ties by start descending, so intervals are processed from 'most constrained' to 'least constrained'.
Track only the two largest chosen integers (a < b); for a new interval, count how many of them fall inside it and add exactly as many new points as needed at the right end of the interval.
Adding points greedily at the right end maximizes their usefulness for later intervals.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over candidate point sets
a.i: Enumerate all pairs of points per interval and search combinations — exponential and impractical, shown only to motivate the greedy. A slightly better brute force tries all subsets of the union of endpoints, checking each interval contains at least two chosen points. This is exponential in the number of distinct coordinates and only feasible for tiny inputs.
s: Collect all distinct endpoint values into a candidate pool.
Iterate subsets of the pool in increasing size order.
For each subset, verify every interval contains at least two chosen points.
a.t: Exponential — enumerating subsets of up to 2n candidates dominates; only viable for toy inputs.
a.sp: O(n) for the candidate pool and bitmask.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy after sorting by end (optimal)
a.i: Sort intervals by end ascending (ties: larger start first). Maintain the two largest chosen points a < b. When processing an interval [s, e]: if b < s we need two new points, take e-1 and e; else if a < s we need one new point, take e; otherwise nothing. Because ties put larger starts first, any later interval with the same end has a smaller-or-equal start, so placing points at the right end never hurts. Each added point is placed as far right as allowed, maximizing overlap with future intervals — this exchange argument proves optimality.
s: Sort intervals by end ascending; break ties by start descending.
Initialize a = -1, b = -1 (two largest chosen points) and answer = 0.
For each interval [s, e]: if b < s, add points e-1 and e, answer += 2, set a = e-1, b = e.
Else if a < s, add point e, answer += 1, set a = b, b = e.
Otherwise the interval already contains a and b; continue.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the scan is O(n).
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond sorting (or O(log n) for the sort stack).

w: In an interview, go straight to the optimal greedy: state the sort order (end asc, start desc), explain why tracking just the two largest points suffices, and argue optimality via an exchange argument (any rightmost-placed point can replace a leftward one without loss). Common pitfalls: forgetting the tie-break on equal ends (breaks correctness when intervals share an endpoint), using strict vs non-strict comparisons incorrectly (points equal to s or e count as inside), and off-by-one when adding e-1/e for a fresh pair. Edge cases: single interval (answer always 2), nested intervals (handled automatically since they're processed after their container when ends tie... actually nested intervals have larger ends and are handled by the a/b checks), duplicate intervals. Follow-ups: generalize to 'at least k points per interval' (keep k largest points, same structure), or stream the intervals instead of sorting them offline.
